w: Behind these warehouse walls sits an estimated $100 billion of art and valuables - the oldest and largest freeport on Earth, its opacity long prized by an elite dodging tax and scrutiny alike. The Panama Papers turned a spotlight on it in 2016, and Switzerland has since passed laws to pry the doors open.
s: The world's biggest vault for hiding art
_facts: World's oldest and largest freeport facility
Holds art estimated at $100 billion, 40% of contents
Scrutinized after 2016 Panama Papers release
New Swiss laws aim to increase transparency

a: Jardin des Alpes, Quai du Mont-Blanc
w: Duke Charles II of Brunswick left his entire fortune to Geneva in 1871 on one condition: build him a mausoleum 'worthy' of him, modeled on the 14th-century Scaliger Tombs in Verona. Marble chimeras and lions guard the white three-tiered result, funded in the same bequest that built the Grand Theatre next door.
s: A duke's fortune bought a copy of Verona's tombs
_facts: Built 1879 in Jardin des Alpes for Charles II, Duke of Brunswick
His 1871 will demanded a mausoleum modeled on Verona's Scaliger Tombs
Same bequest funded the Grand Theatre de Geneve
Guarded by marble chimeras and lions by sculptor Auguste Cain

w: Ancient trees tower over Geneva's largest rose garden inside this 200,000-square-metre park south of the lake, alongside an alpine garden, two theatres and an 18th-century villa. It's the kind of green space that feels older and grander than its city-park billing suggests.
_facts: 200,000 m2 park south of Lake Geneva
Home to Geneva's largest rose garden
Includes an alpine garden, two theatres, an 18th-century villa

w: Built as a lakeside hotel in the 1870s, this five-storey building became the League of Nations' first headquarters in 1920, years before the grander Palais des Nations was finished. Renamed for US President Woodrow Wilson, it survived a 1987 fire in its annex and now houses the UN's human rights office.
s: A hotel that became the League of Nations' first home
_facts: Built 1873-1875 as the Hotel National
Became League of Nations HQ 1920-1936
Named after President Woodrow Wilson in 1924
Annex destroyed by fire in 1987; now UN human rights HQ

w: Opera didn't arrive easily in Calvinist Geneva - the city's first opera house wasn't built until the 1760s. This one opened in 1876 towering over Place Neuve, burned nearly to the ground in 1951, and reopened in 1962 with the largest stage in Switzerland behind its restored facade.
s: Switzerland's largest stage, rebuilt from a fire
_facts: Opened 1876, largest stage in Switzerland
Partly destroyed by fire in 1951, reopened 1962
Geneva's first opera house, Theatre de Rosimond, dates to the 1760s

w: Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret raised this eight-storey block of 45 free-plan apartments in 1931-32, an early test run for ideas that became the Unite d'Habitation. Threatened with demolition twice - the 1960s and early 1980s - it was listed as a historic monument in 1986 and named a UNESCO site in 2016.
s: Le Corbusier's flats, saved twice from demolition
_facts: Designed by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, built 1931-32
Eight storeys, 45 free-plan apartment units
Escaped demolition in the 1960s and early 1980s
Listed historic monument 1986; UNESCO World Heritage Site 2016

w: Collector Gustave Revilliod built this Neo-Classical and Neo-Baroque museum between 1877 and 1884 to house his private hoard of ceramics and glass, then named it Ariana after his mother and bequeathed the lot to Geneva. Around 20,000 objects span 1,200 years - the only collection of its kind in the country.
_facts: Built 1877-1884 by Gustave Revilliod
Named after his mother, Ariane de la Rive
Around 20,000 ceramic and glass objects spanning 1,200 years
Only collection of its kind in Switzerland

n: Basilica of Our Lady of Geneva
w: This Catholic basilica marks the starting point of the Via Gebennensis, one of the pilgrim routes converging on Santiago de Compostela, stretching all the way to Le Puy-en-Velay. A common stopover for pilgrims ever since, it remains a working shrine to the Virgin Mary in a famously Protestant city.
s: Where Compostela pilgrims begin their walk
_facts: Roman Catholic minor basilica dedicated to the Virgin Mary
Marks the start of the Via Gebennensis pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela
Route extends to Le Puy-en-Velay

w: Since 1862 this 250-metre bridge has linked Geneva's left and right banks, named for the distant Alpine massif visible on a clear day. It marks the exact spot where Lake Geneva narrows into the Rhone - officially, the water is called lake on one side of the bridge and river on the other.
s: The bridge where the lake becomes a river
_facts: Inaugurated 1862, about 250 metres long
Named for Mont Blanc, visible from Geneva
Marks transition between Lake Geneva and the Rhone on the Swiss national map

w: This cobblestone square in Geneva's Old Town sits on the site of the ancient Roman forum and a medieval market, then served as a 19th-century stagecoach stop. Today cafe tables ring an 18th-century marble fountain, just steps from St. Pierre Cathedral - centuries of commerce compressed into one small square.
s: A Roman forum turned 19th-century stagecoach stop
_facts: Site of the old Roman forum and medieval market
Served as a 19th-century stagecoach stop
Small marble 18th-century fountain at its centre
Near St. Pierre Cathedral

w: Completed in 1859 for Geneva's Ashkenazi Jewish community - just 200 people at the time - this Great Synagogue still stands at the heart of the city on the square that bears its name. It remains an active congregation more than a century and a half later.
s: The Great Synagogue, built for 200 people
_facts: Completed 1859
Built for Ashkenazi Jewish community of about 200 people
Located at 11 Place de la Synagogue

w: Laid out in 1855 on the site of an old harbor and wood, this lakeside park took its trapezoid shape in 1863 when the Mont-Blanc Bridge went up alongside it. Its flower clock and a bronze fountain by Alexis Andre are local landmarks, and every winter the park hosts Geneva's Christmas market.
_facts: Created 1855 on the site of an ancient harbor and wood
Took its trapezoid shape (25,430 m2) in 1863
Home to the Flower Clock and a bronze fountain by Alexis Andre
Hosts the annual Geneva Christmas Market

w: More than 650,000 objects - archaeology, applied arts, horology, fine art - fill this encyclopedic museum, one of the largest collections in Switzerland. It heads a whole family of Geneva museums, from the porcelain of the Ariana to the timepieces of the Musee de l'Horlogerie, all tracing back to this one institution.
_facts: Collection of more than 650,000 objects
One of the largest museum collections in Switzerland
Heads the association of Geneva's art and history museums, including Ariana and Musee Rath

w: Switzerland's largest natural history museum holds more than 15 million specimens across four floors - nearly half the country's entire natural history collection - including its best-known resident, a two-headed tortoise named Janus. Free to enter since its founding, it's currently closed for renovation.
_facts: Largest natural history museum in Switzerland
Holds more than 15 million specimens across four floors
Home to two-headed tortoise Janus
Closed since January 2024 for renovation

w: Despite its name, no kings are buried here - the Cemetery of Kings takes its name from the Rue des Rois running alongside it. Established in 1482 for victims of the Black Death, the graveyard in Plainpalais has quietly outlasted the epidemic it was built to bury.
s: A plague cemetery named for a street
_facts: Officially called Cimetiere de Plainpalais
Name comes from adjacent Rue des Rois, not royalty
Established 1482 for plague victims of the second plague pandemic

w: Financed by the Saudi-based Muslim World League and completed in 1978, this is the largest mosque in Geneva and in all of Switzerland, with room for 1,500 worshippers. Its inauguration drew both Saudi Arabia's King Khalid and the Swiss president - a rare joint ribbon-cutting for a house of prayer.
_facts: Financed by the Muslim World League, built 1978
Largest mosque in Geneva and Switzerland, capacity 1,500
Inaugurated by King Khalid of Saudi Arabia and Swiss President Willi Ritschard

w: Founded in 1817 by botanist Augustin Pyramus de Candolle, these 28 hectares hold more than 11,000 living plant species and a herbarium of six million pressed specimens - one of the largest in the world. In 2023 it drew roughly 700,000 visits, making it, improbably, Geneva's single most-visited attraction.
s: The city's most-visited attraction is a garden
_facts: Founded 1817 by Augustin Pyramus de Candolle
Covers 28 hectares, more than 11,000 taxa in living collections
Herbarium holds over six million specimens
About 700,000 visits in 2023, city's most visited attraction

w: Gold onion domes and striped Byzantine arches mark this Russian Orthodox cathedral, completed in 1866 in the once-fashionable Tranchees neighborhood. Designed by David Grimm of the Imperial Academy of Arts, it was restored in 1966 and remains an active parish, a world away from its Calvinist surroundings.
s: Byzantine onion domes in a Calvinist city
_facts: Officially Cathedral of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross
Designed by David Grimm, completed 1866
Byzantine revival style with striped arches and gold onion domes
Restored in 1966, remains active
